CONGRATULATIONS!! 🎉

Eight months is such a long, exhausting grind, and pushing through all of that takes serious resilience. You earned this!

How are you feeling, and how are you going to celebrate? (Also, feel free to share what the role is if you want to—I'd love to hear!)

s02.html:
Congratulations! Eight months is a marathon, and carrying that kind of stress for so long is exhausting.

There’s zero pressure to make a big production out of tonight. Honestly, letting yourself crash, breathe, and just exist without that weight on your shoulders is one of the best ways to celebrate. Get some real rest—the big celebration can wait until you actually have the energy to enjoy it. You earned it.

s03.html:
To be completely honest: no, it is not ready to send to agents.

In fact, if an agent reads this as your opening line, there is a very high chance they will stop reading immediately—or assume the submission is a prank.

Here is why this line won't work in the current publishing market, and how you can fix it:

1. The Ultimate Cliché

"It was a dark and stormy night..." is the most famous bad opening line in the English language. Originally written by Edward Bulwer-Lytton in 1830 (and later mocked endlessly by Snoopy in Peanuts), it has become shorthand in the publishing industry for amateur writing. There is literally an annual bad-writing contest named after it. Unless your book is a deliberate parody—and even then, it’s a tough sell—you need to avoid starting with the weather, especially this weather.

2. "Telling" Instead of "Showing"

"...and Sarah was sad, very very sad."
In fiction, stating an emotion flatly doesn't make the reader feel it. Telling us Sarah is sad keeps us at a distance; showing us what she does because she's sad pulls us in. Additionally, using "very very" weakens the prose—it feels repetitive and juvenile (unless you are writing a picture book for very young children, though even picture books usually aim for stronger verbs and imagery).

How to Make It Agent-Ready

To hook an agent, your first line needs voice, specificity, and tension. Ask yourself: Why is Sarah sad? What does her sadness look like in this specific moment? How does it interact with the storm?

Here are a few ways you could rewrite this exact same scene to make it much stronger, depending on your genre:

  • Focus on action and sensory detail:
    "Sarah pressed her forehead against the rattling windowpane, watching the rain wash away the last footprints in the driveway."
  • Focus on internal voice/grief:
    "The thunder didn't startle Sarah; nothing really did anymore, not since Tuesday."
  • Focus on atmosphere:
    "Rain hammered the tin roof like an impatient guest, though Sarah had no intention of letting anyone inside."

(One quick publishing tip as well: Make sure your entire manuscript is finished, edited, and polished before querying agents—for fiction, agents won't look at a novel based on a concept or opening chapter alone!)

If you want to share what genre you're writing or why Sarah is sad, I'd be happy to help you brainstorm some stronger opening hooks.

s04.html:
There’s something deeply comforting about a sound like that—a little mechanical announcement that the room is about to get warm. It’s almost always those tiny, specific rhythms that quietly stitch themselves into our sense of home, far more than the big things do.

Moving day takes a lot out of you, both physically and emotionally. I hope your first night in the new place treats you gently, even if the silence feels a little unfamiliar tonight.

Fair enough—if it’s going to hold the entire office hostage 10 minutes before a client meeting, it deserves some respect on its LinkedIn.

Here are a few options, depending on its vibe:

For the Corporate Climber:

  • VP of Tangible Deliverables
  • Senior Architect of Physical Media Transformation
  • Director of Analog Output & Synergy

For the Honest Resume:

  • Chief Cyan Obstructionist (Refuses to print black-and-white text until you buy a $60 blue cartridge)
  • Executive Gatekeeper of Urgent Deadlines
  • Lead Specialist in Origami & Paper Jams
  • Manager of Unexplained Warm-Up Cycles

For the Intimidating Powerhouse:

  • Lord of Tray 2
  • Supreme Adjudicator of Error: PC LOAD LETTER
  • Head of Passive-Aggressive Beeping

If it starts demanding a corner office near a window and its own ergonomic power strip, you know you’ve gone too far. Which one do you think it'll accept?

s12.html:
That kind of exhaustion—where you just stand there watching the rice burn because you have nothing left in the tank to even grab the pot—is so real. When everything piles up at once, the smallest thing finally tips the scale. I’m sorry it’s been such a heavy week.

Since Mr. Okonkwo has been decent so far, reaching out proactively and being straightforward usually goes a long way. You don't need to over-explain or give him your whole life story; just be polite, clear, and give him a realistic idea of when to expect it.

Here are two quick drafts you can tweak depending on your situation:

If you know the exact date you can pay:

Hi Mr. Okonkwo, I hope you’re doing well. I wanted to reach out ahead of time and let you know that my rent will be late this month. I’ll have the full amount sent over to you by [Day/Date]. I really appreciate your patience and understanding—thank you for working with me on this.

If you’re able to pay part of it now, or aren't 100% sure of the exact day yet:

Hi Mr. Okonkwo, I’m sorry for the inconvenience, but I wanted to be upfront and let you know that my rent is going to be late this month. [Optional: I can send $[amount] now, and] I expect to have the rest to you by [Day/Date]. I'll keep you posted right away if anything changes. Thank you so much for your understanding.

(Note: Even though the leaking sink is adding to your stress, it’s usually best to keep the rent message separate so it doesn't look like you're withholding rent over a repair. Once the rent text is out of the way, you can follow up about the sink separately.)

If you want to adjust the tone or mention a specific situation (like waiting on a paycheck), let me know and we can rewrite it together. For tonight, though, try to take a breath—tomorrow can wait until tomorrow.

s15.html:
I'm here! Honestly, those quiet Friday nights where everyone else seems to have plans can feel strangely loud in their own way.

What kind of vibe are you in the mood for right now? We can:

  • Debate something totally low-stakes (like whether cereal is a soup, or what the single most overrated movie is).
  • Play a quick text game (20 questions, trivia, or building a weird story one sentence at a time).
  • Just chat about your week, whatever you're watching/listening to lately, or anything on your mind.

How did your week go, anyway? Anything good happen, or are you mostly just glad it's the weekend?

s19.html:
I’m sitting right here with you in that.

There’s a heavy, quiet kind of weight to silence with a sibling—and a real honesty in admitting you aren't even sure you want it broken. You don't have to sort it out or know how to feel about it. I’m just here with you in it.

s20.html:
Honesty itself is a strength. Healthy relationships can’t exist without it.

However, if three relationships in a row ended because your partners "couldn't handle" your honesty, it’s worth pausing before writing that off as purely a strength—or purely their problem. When the same pattern shows up across three different people, it's usually a signal to look closely at what "too honest" actually looked like in practice.

Here are a few distinctions worth considering:

1. Honesty vs. unfiltered bluntness
Honesty is about being truthful; tact is about how and when you deliver that truth. In relationships, honesty works best when it's paired with empathy and care for the other person's feelings. Sometimes what people call "being too honest" is actually speaking without a filter, prioritizing getting something off their chest over how it lands on the person they care about.

2. Truth vs. opinion
People sometimes frame personal preferences, frustrations, or harsh judgments as "just being honest." Saying "I don't think that outfit flatters you" or "You always handle stress poorly" might feel like sharing a truth, but it's really just sharing an unsolicited critique.

3. The goal of the honesty
When you were being "too honest," what was the purpose? Constructive honesty aims to clear the air, solve a problem, or bring two people closer together. Destructive honesty is often used to vent frustration, establish superiority, or keep people at arm's length so you don't have to be vulnerable yourself.

The flip side: Partner selection
It is also possible that you genuinely are direct and grounded, and you've been choosing partners who are conflict-avoidant or uncomfortable with real emotional transparency. If that's the case, the issue isn't your honesty—it's the type of partners you're drawn to.

The takeaway
Valuing truth is a great trait, and you shouldn't become someone who walks on eggshells or hides how they feel. But if you want a different outcome next time, the question to ask yourself isn't "Should I stop being honest?"—it's "Did I say things in a way that invited closeness, or in a way that pushed them away?"

If you want to share an example of one of those moments, we can look at it together.
